title: Build an Investigation Tool
content:
What problem does this solve?
When the same labeling or decision appears in many places, copy-pasting code becomes fragile. A function packages a reusable action under a name so the rest of the program can call it.

Basic syntax
  def mark_evidence(clue):
      return f"Evidence: {clue}"

What actually happens
def creates a function and binds it to a name. Calling mark_evidence("broken lantern") assigns that string to the parameter clue, runs the body, and return sends a value back to the caller. You have already been calling print and append; now you define a name other code can call.

Critical distinction
  print(result)  — shows something to a human
  return result  — gives a value to other code

If you only print inside a function, callers cannot use the computed value in further calculations or later print calls of their own.

When this is useful
Use a function when a calculation or decision will be needed more than once, or when another piece of code must receive the result. This lesson stays small: one parameter, return, and calls — deeper function ideas come later.
concepts: A parameter receives the argument value for one call
return sends a value to the caller; print only displays
Callers can store or print a returned value

examples.title: Reusable evidence label
examples.code:
def mark_evidence(clue):
    return f"Evidence: {clue}"

result = mark_evidence("broken lantern")
print(result)
examples.explanation: mark_evidence returns a string. The caller stores it in result, then prints it.

examples.title: Print versus return
examples.explanation: Printing shows text to a human. Returning gives a value other code can use.

common_mistakes: Using print instead of return, then wondering why the caller received None
Forgetting parentheses when calling: mark_evidence "clue" is invalid
Hardcoding one answer instead of using the parameter

exercises.title: Predict the function call
hints: Trace the call: the argument becomes the parameter clue.
return builds a string; print displays what came back.
The finished line is Evidence: broken lantern.

exercises.title: print or return?
exercises.prompt: Another part of the investigation program must use the generated status line — store it, compare it, or print it later. Should the function print that status, or return it?
choices: Only print the status inside the function
Return the status so callers can use it
exercises.success_message: Right — other code can only keep working with the status if the function returns it.
exercises.failure_message: Printed text is for humans. If later code must use the generated status, the function needs to return that string.
hints: Ask whether another part of the program needs the text as a value.
Printed text is for humans; returned values are for programs.
Choose the option that returns the status.

exercises.title: Write inspect_clue()
exercises.prompt:
Write inspect_clue(clue) that returns:
  FLAG: gray dust  when clue is "gray dust"
  logged: <clue>   for every other clue

Use one parameter, if/else, an f-string, and return. Do not print inside the function — return the text so callers can use it.
hints: Compare clue with the string "gray dust", then return one of two labeled lines.
Use return with an f-string in each branch — not print.
if clue == "gray dust": return f"FLAG: {clue}" else return f"logged: {clue}".

tests.message: Use if/else inside inspect_clue to choose FLAG or logged.
Build the returned lines with an f-string.

exercises.success_message: inspect_clue works across several clues — including the flagged gray dust.

exercises.title: The Expedition 17 Report
exercises.prompt:
Build the Expedition 17 evidence report.

1. Define inspect_clue(clue).
2. If clue is "gray dust", return FLAG: <clue>.
3. Otherwise return logged: <clue>.
4. Loop through every item in the supplied evidence list.
5. Call inspect_clue() for each item.
6. Print what the function returns.

Expected output:
logged: broken lantern
FLAG: gray dust
logged: torn cloak

No new syntax — combine a list, for loop, function, if/else, f-string, return, and print.
exercises.starter_code:
evidence = [
    "broken lantern",
    "gray dust",
    "torn cloak",
]

# Define inspect_clue, then loop and print each result
hints: Define inspect_clue first so the loop can call it for each clue.
Inside the loop, print the value returned by inspect_clue(clue) — do not rebuild the labels only in the loop.
A solid shape: define inspect_clue with if/else and return, then for clue in evidence: print(inspect_clue(clue)).

tests.name: inspect_clue
tests.message: Call inspect_clue(clue) from inside the evidence for-loop body (a dummy call elsewhere is not enough).
Use a for loop to visit every evidence item.
Use if/else inside inspect_clue (or clearly in the scan) to flag gray dust.
Build FLAG/logged lines with an f-string.

tests.expected:
logged: broken lantern
FLAG: gray dust
logged: torn cloak

exercises.success_message: Expedition 17 report complete. You combined variables, lists, loops, decisions, f-strings, and functions into one investigation tool.
